governanceNotes: Authored conservatively as ASSOCIATION_ONLY: systematic reviews and meta-analyses report substantially higher anxiety (and depression) prevalence among BPPV and other vestibular-disorder patients than controls, but the evidence is cross-sectional or cohort-level with acknowledged bidirectionality (anxiety can amplify dizziness handicap and vestibular symptoms), so the mapping cannot assert causation or aggravation for any individual.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of observational studies report that patients with BPPV show significantly higher anxiety prevalence than controls (roughly threefold increased odds in one meta-analysis, with about a quarter of BPPV patients affected), and a large vestibular-disorder meta-analysis reports elevated anxiety across episodic vestibular conditions including BPPV, with dizziness-handicap scores correlating with anxiety measures.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the cited meta-analyses pool cross-sectional and cohort studies that cannot establish direction, the included reviews explicitly call for further studies to confirm the associations, anxiety disorders can amplify or maintain dizziness symptoms independently of peripheral vestibular status, and shared drivers (inner-ear disease, medical comorbidity, psychosocial stressors) require individual exclusion.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized vestibular-anxiety coupling pathway has been described: recurrent unpredictable positional vertigo episodes can condition anticipatory anxiety and postural-control vigilance, and shared vestibular-anxiety circuitry (including noradrenergic pathways) has been proposed to explain the comorbidity, but this coupling would explain co-occurrence without establishing that BPPV caused an anxiety disorder in any individual, and reverse causation (anxiety amplifying symptom perception) remains an active competing explanation, so no directional claim is made here.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Meta-analytic evidence reports higher anxiety prevalence among BPPV patients with dizziness-handicap correlation, but individual determination requires otolaryngology or vestibular documentation of BPPV (Dix-Hallpike confirmation) with chronology, separate psychiatric diagnosis of an anxiety disorder, and exclusion of competing explanations, all reviewed case by case by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Vestibular-clinic documentation of BPPV diagnosis (positioning-test confirmation) with episode chronology; psychiatric diagnosis of an anxiety disorder against accepted criteria at a defined time point; dizziness-handicap and anxiety-severity measures at relevant time points; treatment-response records (canalith repositioning and anxiety outcomes); competing-explanation review including panic disorder and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Preexisting or independent anxiety disorder unrelated to vestibular symptoms
Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness or panic disorder as the unifying diagnosis
Meniere-syndrome, vestibular migraine, or other vestibular diagnoses driving both symptoms
Medication effects (vestibular suppressants) contributing to mood symptoms

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the meta-analytic anxiety association in BPPV is well supported but cross-sectional, with explicit calls for confirmatory studies and acknowledged bidirectionality, so this edge flags the comorbidity for evidence-gap review only and must never be presented as established causation or aggravation.
evidenceGaps: Positioning-test-confirmed BPPV diagnosis with episode chronology
Psychiatric assessment establishing an anxiety disorder with temporality
Dizziness-handicap and anxiety-severity documentation at relevant time points
A medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case

sourceReferences.citation: Yeo BSY, Toh EMS, Lim NE, Lee RS, Ho RCM, Tam WWS, Ngo RYS. Association of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo with Depression and Anxiety-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Laryngoscope. 2024;134(2):526-534. PMID 37560919. doi:10.1002/lary.30957.
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review and meta-analysis reporting BPPV associated with roughly threefold increased anxiety risk and elevated anxiety inventory scores; explicitly calls for further studies to confirm the association, supporting the bounded association-only framing rather than individual causation.

sourceReferences.note: Large vestibular-disorder meta-analysis reporting elevated anxiety prevalence across episodic vestibular conditions including BPPV with dizziness-handicap correlation; supports the syndrome-level comorbidity proposition and the bidirectionality caution, not a directional causal claim.
